concepts.title: Shearing Transformation
concepts.one_liner: Shearing involves scale factors in the off-diagonal matrix locations, displacing points along lines by a distance proportional to their coordinate.
concepts.content:
Shearing involves scale factors in the off-diagonal matrix locations, as shown in the matrix $\mathbf{Q}$:

$$\mathbf{Q} =             
    \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & q_x & 0 \\
    q_y & 1 & 0 \\
    0 & 0 & 1
    \end{bmatrix}$$

(see figure: Three examples of shear transformation.)

In the example of a horizontal shear ($q_x=1, q_y=0$), points are displaced along horizontal lines by a displacement proportional to the $y$ coordinate, $x'=x+q_y y$. In a shear, lines are mapped to lines and parallel lines remain parallel, but (non-zero) angles between lines change.
concepts.motivation_md: Shearing is used to skew or tilt an image or object. It allows for transformations where parallel lines are preserved but the relative angles between axes change, which is useful for simulating perspective or creating italicized effects.

concepts.title: Chaining Transformations
concepts.one_liner: Complex geometric operations can be built by multiplying the matrices of individual transformations in a specific order.
concepts.motivation_md: Chaining allows for the creation of complex movements and orientations by breaking them down into simple, fundamental operations like translation, rotation, and scaling.
concepts.recap_md:
- Complex transformations are achieved through matrix multiplication.
- The order of operations matters because matrix multiplication is noncommutative.
- To transform around a specific point, translate that point to the origin first.

concepts.title: Euclidean Transformation
concepts.one_liner: A Euclidean transformation is the result of chaining rotations and translations, preserving both lengths and angles.
concepts.content: When chaining rotations and translations only, we will have a euclidean transformation. In this type of transformation, lengths and angles between lines are preserved.
concepts.motivation_md: Euclidean transformations represent rigid body motions where the shape and size of an object do not change, only its position and orientation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Formed by chaining only rotations and translations.
- Preserves both lengths and angles between lines.

slots.motivation: Euclidean transformations represent rigid body motions where the shape and size of an object do not change, only its position and orientation.

- Preserves both lengths and angles between lines.

concepts.title: Similarity Transform
concepts.one_liner: A similarity transform chains rotation, translation, and uniform scaling, preserving angles but not lengths.
concepts.content: A similarity transform is the result of chaining a rotation, translation, and scaling (specifically with uniform scaling, where $s_x=s_y$). In this case, angles are preserved but lengths are not.
concepts.motivation_md: Similarity transforms are used when an object's shape must be maintained while its size and position change, such as zooming in on a map.
concepts.recap_md:
- Combines rotation, translation, and uniform scaling.
- Preserves angles but changes lengths.

concepts.title: Affine Transformation
concepts.one_liner: An affine transformation chains translations, scalings, rotations, and shears, preserving parallel lines but not necessarily lengths or angles.
concepts.content:
Chaining translations, scalings, rotations, and shears results in an affine transformation. In general, this results in a generic matrix with the form:

$$\mathbf{p}' = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    a & b & c \\
    d & e & f \\
    0 & 0 & 1
    \end{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{p}$$

Any transformation with this form (6 degrees of freedom) is an affine transformation. An affine transformation has the property that parallel lines will remain parallel after the transformation; however, lengths and non-zero angles might change.
concepts.motivation_md: Affine transformations provide a flexible way to map coordinates while maintaining linear structures, which is essential for image registration and computer graphics.
concepts.recap_md:
- Includes translations, scalings, rotations, and shears.
- Parallel lines remain parallel after transformation.
- Represented by a matrix with 6 degrees of freedom.

slots.motivation: Affine transformations provide a flexible way to map coordinates while maintaining linear structures, which is essential for image registration and computer graphics.

- Parallel lines remain parallel after transformation.
- Represented by a matrix with 6 degrees of freedom.

concepts.title: Projective Transformation
concepts.one_liner: Projective transformations use a full 3x3 matrix with 8 degrees of freedom to represent more general geometric mappings.
concepts.content:
A projective transformation occurs when we use a full $3 \times 3$ matrix with 9 parameters:

$$\mathbf{p}' = 
    \begin{bmatrix}
    a & b & c \\
    d & e & f \\
    g & h & i
    \end{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{p}$$

In fact, we only have 8 degrees of freedom because a global scaling of the matrix does not change the homogeneous coordinates. This set of transformations is more general than affine transformations and includes elations.
concepts.motivation_md: Projective transformations are necessary to model how 3D scenes are projected onto 2D surfaces, accounting for perspective effects where parallel lines appear to converge.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses a full matrix with 8 degrees of freedom.
- More general than affine transformations.
- Global scaling of the matrix does not affect the result in homogeneous coordinates.

concepts.title: Elation
concepts.one_liner: An elation is a specific type of projective transformation arising from the additional degrees of freedom in a full transformation matrix.
concepts.content: Elations are a subset of transformations described by the full $3 \times 3$ projective matrix. They represent additional degrees of freedom beyond those found in affine transformations.
concepts.motivation_md: Elations are specific projective transformations used in geometry to describe mappings that fix all points on a line and all lines through a point on that line.
concepts.recap_md:
- A type of projective transformation.
- Enabled by the 8 degrees of freedom in a general homogeneous matrix.

concepts.title: Geometric Transformations as Convolutions
concepts.one_liner: When geometry is explicitly added to image representation, transformations like rotations and shears can be implemented as 1D convolutions over locations.
concepts.content:
Once geometry is added to the image representation, transformations such as rotations, scalings, and shears can be implemented as one-dimensional (1D) convolutions over the locations.

(see figure: Geometric transformation as a convolution. The input and output signals are represented as pixel sets with explicit geometry. The convolution kernels are $w_x$ and $w_y$, corresponding to one...)

In this representation, each input element is a vector $(x_i, y_i, \ell_i)$ where $x_i, y_i$ are the pixel location and $\ell_i$ is the pixel intensity. The convolution kernels are $w_x = [\cos(\theta), \sin(\theta)]$ and $w_y = [-\sin(\theta), \cos(\theta)]$. The weights are the same for all inputs, and the output is also represented using explicit positions $(x'_i, y'_i, \ell'_i)$. Note that performing a convolution on the output intensity requires translating the position encoding back into a rectangular grid, as transformations like rotation move pixels off the original grid.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach unifies geometric transformations and signal processing, allowing complex spatial changes to be treated with the same mathematical framework as linear filtering.
concepts.recap_md:
- Transformations are modeled as 1D convolutions over coordinate vectors $(x, y, \ell)$.
- Convolution kernels like $w_x$ and $w_y$ apply the transformation weights to all inputs.
- Output positions must be re-mapped to a rectangular grid for standard image processing.

- Convolution kernels like $w_x$ and $w_y$ apply the transformation weights to all inputs.
- Output positions must be re-mapped to a rectangular grid for standard image processing.

concepts.title: Image Representation: Set of Pixels
concepts.one_liner: An image can be represented as a collection of points, indicating its color and location explicitly as a set of pixels.
concepts.content: An image can be represented as a collection of points, indicating its color and location explicitly. In this case, an image is represented as a **set of pixels**: $$\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i,y_i] : i \right\}$$ where $\ell_i$ is the pixel intensity (or color) recorded at location $(x_i,y_i)$. This representation makes the geometry explicit. While it might seem like a trivial representation, it makes some operations easy. For instance, we can apply geometric transformations easily by directly working with the spatial coordinates. If you want to translate an image to the right by one pixel, you can do that easily by simply creating the new image defined by the set of translated pixels: $\left\{ [\ell_i,x_i+1,y_i] : i \right\}$. Representing images as sets of points is very common in geometry-based computer vision.
concepts.motivation_md: This representation makes the geometric properties of an image explicit, facilitating operations like spatial transformations (translation, rotation) that are more complex in standard grid-based formats.
concepts.recap_md: - An image is defined as a set of tuples containing intensity and spatial coordinates.

slots.motivation: This representation makes the geometric properties of an image explicit, facilitating operations like spatial transformations (translation, rotation) that are more complex in standard grid-based formats.
slots.key_passage: - An image is defined as a set of tuples containing intensity and spatial coordinates.

Representing images as sets of points is very common in geometry-based computer vision.

concepts.title: Image Representation: Continuous Function
concepts.one_liner: An image can be represented as a continuous function whose input is a location and whose output is an intensity or color.
concepts.content: Another option is to represent an image as a continuous function whose input is a location $(x, y)$ and whose output is an intensity, or a color, $\ell$: $$\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$$ This image representation is commonly used when we want to make image priors more explicit. The function $f_{\theta}$ is parameterized by the coefficients $\theta$. This function becomes especially interesting when the parameters $\theta$ are different than the original pixel values, requiring them to be estimated from the original image. Once learned, the function $f$ should be able to take as input continuous spatial variables.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing images as continuous functions allows for the use of continuous spatial variables and makes image priors explicit, which is useful for tasks like super-resolution or image modeling.
concepts.recap_md: - Images are modeled as functions $f_{\theta}(x,y)$ mapping coordinates to intensities.

slots.motivation: Representing images as continuous functions allows for the use of continuous spatial variables and makes image priors explicit, which is useful for tasks like super-resolution or image modeling.
slots.key_passage: - Images are modeled as functions $f_{\theta}(x,y)$ mapping coordinates to intensities.

concepts.title: Homogeneous Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: Homogeneous coordinates represent a vector of length $N$ by a vector of length $N+1$, where all non-zero scalings are equivalent.
concepts.content: Homogeneous coordinates represent a vector of length $N$ by a vector of length $N+1$. The transformation rule from heterogeneous to homogeneous coordinates is simply to add an additional coordinate, 1, to the heterogeneous coordinates: $$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ It is the same if the vector has three dimensions: $$\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Homogeneous coordinates have the additional rule that all (non-zero) scalings of a homogeneous coordinate vector are equivalent: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} \lambda x \\ \lambda y \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix}$$ for any non-zero scalar, $\lambda$. To go from homogeneous coordinates back to the heterogeneous representation, we divide all the entries of the homogeneous coordinate vector by their last dimension: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ w \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} x/w \\ y/w \end{pmatrix}$$ A point in homogeneous coordinates is scale invariant, which is closely related to perspective projection. (see figure: Transformation rule between heterogeneous and homogeneous coordinates in 2D. All the points along the dotted line correspond to the same point in heterogeneous coordinates. Note that the points...) While you can add two points in heterogeneous coordinates, you cannot do the same in homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Homogeneous coordinates simplify geometric transformations like translation and perspective projection by allowing them to be expressed as linear matrix multiplications.
concepts.recap_md: - Convert to homogeneous by appending a 1; convert back by dividing by the last coordinate.

concepts.title: Heterogeneous Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: Heterogeneous coordinates are conventional Cartesian coordinate descriptions of points in 2D or 3D space.
concepts.content: Heterogeneous coordinates refer to conventional Cartesian coordinate descriptions of a point in 2D, such as $(x,y)$, or 3D, such as $(x,y,z)$. In mathematical notation, these are typically written with rounded brackets, whereas their corresponding homogeneous coordinate representations are denoted by square bracketed vectors.
concepts.motivation_md: These are the standard coordinates used in Euclidean geometry to represent positions in space relative to an origin.
concepts.recap_md: - Standard Cartesian coordinates like $(x, y)$ or $(x, y, z)$. - Typically denoted with rounded brackets to distinguish them from homogeneous vectors.

slots.motivation: These are the standard coordinates used in Euclidean geometry to represent positions in space relative to an origin.

In mathematical notation, these are typically written with rounded brackets, whereas their corresponding homogeneous coordinate representations are denoted by square bracketed vectors.

concepts.title: Scaling Invariance of Homogeneous Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: In homogeneous coordinates, all non-zero scalings of a coordinate vector are equivalent and represent the same point.
concepts.content: The homogeneous coordinates have the rule that all (non-zero) scalings of a homogeneous coordinate vector are equivalent. For example, to represent a 2D point, we have: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} \lambda x \\ \lambda y \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix}$$ for any non-zero scalar, $\lambda$. This property implies that a point in homogeneous coordinates is scale invariant, meaning any point within the line that passes through the origin translates into the same point in heterogeneous coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Scaling invariance allows the representation of points at infinity and simplifies the math of perspective projection, where distance from the camera scales the observed coordinates.
concepts.recap_md: - Multiplying a homogeneous vector by a non-zero scalar does not change the point it represents.

slots.key_passage: - Multiplying a homogeneous vector by a non-zero scalar does not change the point it represents.

For example, to represent a 2D point, we have: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} \lambda x \\ \lambda y \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix}$$ for any non-zero scalar, $\lambda$. This property implies that a point in homogeneous coordinates is scale invariant, meaning any point within the line that passes through the origin translates into the same point in heterogeneous coordinates.

concepts.title: Conversion from Homogeneous to Heterogeneous Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: To convert from homogeneous to heterogeneous coordinates, divide all entries of the vector by its last dimension.
concepts.content: To go from homogeneous coordinates back to the heterogeneous representation of a point, we divide all the entries of the homogeneous coordinate vector by their last dimension: $$\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ w \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} x/w \\ y/w \end{pmatrix}$$ This normalization step recovers the standard Cartesian coordinates from the projective representation.
concepts.motivation_md: This conversion is necessary to extract physical spatial coordinates from the projective space used during matrix transformations.
concepts.recap_md: - Divide every component of the vector by the final coordinate $w$.

slots.key_passage: - Divide every component of the vector by the final coordinate $w$.

concepts.title: 2D Translation in Homogeneous Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: Translation in homogeneous coordinates is represented as a matrix-vector product rather than vector addition.
concepts.content: Consider a translation by a 2D vector $(t_x, t_y)$. In heterogeneous coordinates, we have $$\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} t_x \\ t_y \end{pmatrix}$$ We can write this translation in homogeneous coordinates by the product: $$ \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} $$ This transforms an addition into a product by a matrix, $\mathbf{T}$, and a vector, $\mathbf{p}$, in homogeneous coordinates: $$ \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{T} \mathbf{p}, $$ with the homogeneous matrix, $\mathbf{T}$, defined as $$ \mathbf{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} $$ For calculations in homogeneous coordinates, both matrices and vectors are only defined up to an arbitrary (non-zero) multiplicative scaling factor. (see figure: (left) Translation. (right) Composition of two consecutive translations.)
concepts.motivation_md: Using homogeneous coordinates allows translations to be treated as linear transformations, enabling the composition of multiple transformations into a single matrix.
concepts.recap_md: - Translation is represented by a matrix with the translation vector in the last column. - This converts the operation from vector addition to matrix multiplication.

slots.motivation: Using homogeneous coordinates allows translations to be treated as linear transformations, enabling the composition of multiple transformations into a single matrix.
slots.key_passage: - Translation is represented by a matrix with the translation vector in the last column. - This converts the operation from vector addition to matrix multiplication.

In heterogeneous coordinates, we have $$\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} t_x \\ t_y \end{pmatrix}$$ We can write this translation in homogeneous coordinates by the product: $$ \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} $$ This transforms an addition into a product by a matrix, $\mathbf{T}$, and a vector, $\mathbf{p}$, in homogeneous coordinates: $$ \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{T} \mathbf{p}, $$ with the homogeneous matrix, $\mathbf{T}$, defined as $$ \mathbf{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & t_x \\ 0 & 1 & t_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} $$ For calculations in homogeneous coordinates, both matrices and vectors are only defined up to an arbitrary (non-zero) multiplicative scaling factor. (see figure: (left) Translation. (right) Composition of two consecutive translations.)

concepts.title: Small Angle Rotation Approximation
concepts.one_liner: For very small angles, the rotation matrix can be approximated using a Taylor development where $\sin(x) \approx x$ and $\cos(x) \approx 1$.
concepts.content: If the angle of rotation is very small, then we can approximate the rotation matrix by its Taylor development: $$\mathbf{R} \simeq \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \theta & 0 \\ -\theta & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ This approximation is valid because for small $x$, $\sin(x) \approx x$ and $\cos(x) \approx 1$. For small angles, a rotation becomes a shear. In general, for all angles, a rotation can be written as two shears and a scaling.
concepts.motivation_md: Small angle approximations simplify the math in iterative algorithms, tracking, or when dealing with incremental changes in orientation.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses the approximations $\sin(\theta) \approx \theta$ and $\cos(\theta) \approx 1$. - The resulting matrix represents a shear operation.

slots.motivation: Small angle approximations simplify the math in iterative algorithms, tracking, or when dealing with incremental changes in orientation.
slots.key_passage: - Uses the approximations $\sin(\theta) \approx \theta$ and $\cos(\theta) \approx 1$. - The resulting matrix represents a shear operation.
slots.example: If the angle of rotation is very small, then we can approximate the rotation matrix by its Taylor development: $$\mathbf{R} \simeq \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \theta & 0 \\ -\theta & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ This approximation is valid because for small $x$, $\sin(x) \approx x$ and $\cos(x) \approx 1$. For small angles, a rotation becomes a shear. In general, for all angles, a rotation can be written as two shears and a scaling.

concepts.title: Image Representation: Ordered Array
concepts.one_liner: The ordered array representation treats images as regular spatial grids of pixel values, typically grayscale intensities or color channels.
concepts.content:
The ordered array is a representation of images as ordered arrays of pixel values, where each pixel is described by its grayscale value (or three arrays for color images). This representation is defined as:
$$\boldsymbol\ell=\left[
\begin{matrix}
\ell[1,1] & \dots & \\
\vdots & \ell[n,m] & \vdots \\
 & \dots  & \ell[N,M] \\
\end{matrix}
\right]$$
Each value is a sample on a regular spatial grid. In this notation, the value represents the pixel intensity at one location. This is the typical representation used from a signal processing perspective and makes it simpler to describe operations such as convolution.
concepts.motivation_md: This representation provides a structured, discrete way to process visual information using standard linear algebra and signal processing techniques like convolution.
concepts.recap_md: - Images are represented as matrices where each entry corresponds to a pixel intensity on a regular grid.

slots.motivation: This representation provides a structured, discrete way to process visual information using standard linear algebra and signal processing techniques like convolution.
slots.key_passage: - Images are represented as matrices where each entry corresponds to a pixel intensity on a regular grid.

concepts.title: Implicit Image Representation
concepts.one_liner: An implicit image representation is a continuous function $f_\theta(x,y)$ trained to reproduce image pixels at any real-valued coordinate.
concepts.content: An image is typically an array of values $\boldsymbol\ell\in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 3}$, where each value is indexed as $\ell[n,m]$ for discrete values of $n$ and $m$. Interpolation transforms this discrete image into a continuous signal $\ell(x,y)$. An implicit image representation uses a function $f_\theta$ trained to reproduce the image pixels such that $\ell(x,y) = f_{\theta}(x,y)$, where $x$ and $y$ can now take on any real value.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional images are stored as discrete grids, which require interpolation algorithms to estimate values between pixels. Representing an image as a continuous function allows for a resolution-independent representation and a unified mathematical treatment of image sampling.
concepts.recap_md: - An implicit representation treats an image as a continuous function $f_\theta(x,y)$ rather than a discrete grid. - This approach allows the image to be evaluated at any real-valued coordinate $(x,y)$.

slots.motivation: Traditional images are stored as discrete grids, which require interpolation algorithms to estimate values between pixels. Representing an image as a continuous function allows for a resolution-independent representation and a unified mathematical treatment of image sampling.

concepts.title: Neural Implicit Image Representation
concepts.one_liner: A neural implicit representation uses a neural network to map image coordinates $(x, y)$ to intensity or color values by memorizing the image pixels.
concepts.content: In the case of nearest neighbors or bilinear interpolation, the parameters of the interpolation function $\theta$ is the input image itself. For example, using a functional form, nearest neighbors interpolation can be written as $\ell(x,y) = \ell\left[ \text{round}(x), \text{round}(y) \right]$. We can extend the space of possible functions $f_{\theta}(x,y)$ to include other functional forms, such as a neural network. This network takes the two image coordinate values $x$ and $y$ as input and outputs the intensity value at that location. The training set for the neural network is the image itself, consisting of input-output pairs $[(x_i, y_i); \ell(x_i,y_i)]$. During training, the neural network memorizes the image; while it only sees discrete positions during training, it can be evaluated at any continuous input value at test time. For this to work, the network must be able to generalize to non-integer coordinate values to interpolate between samples.
concepts.motivation_md: By using a neural network as the interpolation function, we can learn complex, continuous representations of images that can generalize between discrete samples and potentially provide more flexible image processing capabilities.
concepts.recap_md: - Neural networks can be trained to memorize an image by mapping coordinates to pixel intensities. - The training set consists of discrete pixel locations and their corresponding colors. - Once trained, the network can interpolate values at any continuous coordinate.

concepts.title: Image Warping with Implicit Representations
concepts.one_liner: Image warping is performed by applying an inverse geometric transformation to output coordinates and evaluating the learned implicit function $f_\theta$ at the resulting locations.
concepts.content: Once the neural network $f_{\theta}(x,y)$ has learned to reproduce the image, we can reconstruct the original image or apply transformations to it. Image warping is implemented by applying the inverse geometric transformation to the discrete coordinates of the output grid and using the functional representation of the image to get the interpolated values: $$\hat{\ell} (x,y) = f_{\theta} \left( \mathbf{M}^{-1}(x,y,1)^\mathsf{T}\right)$$ In this equation, the input location is written in homogeneous coordinates, so the function $f$ must first divide by the third component to translate the input back to heterogeneous coordinates. (see figure: A grayscale photograph of a man in a dark coat looking through a camera mounted on a tripod in an open field. This is the classic 'cameraman' test image, used here to demonstrate image reconstruction...) (see figure: A grayscale image of a cameraman on a tripod, which has been rotated and scaled within a larger frame. The area outside the original image boundaries is filled with a smooth, cloud-like noise pattern...) The example above shows an image encoded by a sinusoidal representation network (SIREN) and then reconstructed with a rotation of 45 degrees and a scaling by 0.5. Observations show that transformations can cause aliasing in the sampled image, which can be avoided by sampling on a finer grid followed by blurring and downsampling. Additionally, the image boundary is padded by a form of noise that smoothly extends the image without adding strong derivatives.
concepts.motivation_md: Implicit representations simplify warping because they provide a continuous function that can be sampled at any transformed coordinate, avoiding the need for explicit grid-based interpolation algorithms during the warp.
concepts.recap_md: - Warping involves mapping output coordinates back to the input space via an inverse transformation $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$. - The implicit function $f_\theta$ is evaluated at these transformed coordinates to produce the warped image. - Implicit representations like SIRENs naturally handle boundary extension with smooth noise rather than standard padding.

concepts.title: Image Alignment
concepts.one_liner: Image alignment is the process of identifying the transformation $\mathbf{M}$ that relates two images, where one is a transformed version of the other.
concepts.content: Image alignment is the reverse problem of image warping. Given two images where one is a transformed version of the other, the goal is to identify the transformation $\mathbf{M}$ that relates them.
concepts.motivation_md: Alignment is a fundamental task in computer vision, necessary for stitching multiple photos into a panorama, tracking objects across video frames, or registering medical scans taken at different times.
concepts.recap_md: - Alignment seeks the transformation matrix $\mathbf{M}$ between two related images. - It is the inverse problem of applying a known transformation to an image.

slots.motivation: Alignment is a fundamental task in computer vision, necessary for stitching multiple photos into a panorama, tracking objects across video frames, or registering medical scans taken at different times.

concepts.title: Spatial Transformer Network
concepts.one_liner: A spatial transformer network uses parametric image transformations within a neural network to align training examples into a canonical pose.
concepts.content: The spatial transformer network is an example of using parametric image transformations inside a neural network. Such transformations can be helpful during learning to align the training examples into a canonical pose.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard convolutional networks are not naturally invariant to large rotations or translations; spatial transformers allow the network to actively transform data to a standard orientation, improving recognition performance.
concepts.recap_md: - Spatial transformers apply learnable geometric transformations to input data within a neural network. - They help align examples into a canonical pose to simplify subsequent learning tasks.

slots.motivation: Standard convolutional networks are not naturally invariant to large rotations or translations; spatial transformers allow the network to actively transform data to a standard orientation, improving recognition performance.

concepts.title: Line Equation in Homogeneous Coordinates

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: In homogeneous coordinates, a 2D line is represented by a vector such that its dot product with any point on the line equals zero.
concepts.content: The equation of a line $ax+by+c=0$ can be written in homogeneous coordinates as: $$ax+by+c=0 \rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = 0$$ In this system, the equation of a line is the dot product $\boldsymbol{l} ^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p} = 0$ where $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}= \left [a, b, c\right ]$. A point $\mathbf{p}$ belongs to the line when $\boldsymbol{l}$ and $\mathbf{p}$ are perpendicular. This representation is scale invariant, meaning $\left [a, b, c\right ]$ represents the same line as $\left [a/c, b/c, 1\right ]$. It is also useful to describe the line using $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}= \left [n_x, n_y, -d\right ]$, where $(n_x,n_y)$ is the normal to the line and $d$ is the distance to the origin.
concepts.motivation_md: Homogeneous coordinates provide a scale-invariant representation of lines, simplifying geometric operations into linear algebra. This allows for a unified treatment of points and lines through dot products and perpendicularity.
concepts.recap_md: - A line is defined by a vector $\boldsymbol{l}$ such that $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p} = 0$ for all points $\mathbf{p}$ on it.

concepts.title: Line from Two Points

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: The line passing through two points in homogeneous coordinates is calculated as the cross product of the points' vectors.
concepts.content: Using homogeneous coordinates makes obtaining geometric properties of points and lines very easy. Given two points $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ in homogeneous coordinates, the line that passes by both points is the cross product: $$\boldsymbol{l} = \mathbf{p}_1 \times \mathbf{p}_2$$ (see figure: Using homogeneous coordinates to get the line that passes by two points, and to obtain the intersection of two lines. Both operations are analogous.) This is because if the line passes by both points, it has to verify that $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}_1=0$ and $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}_2=0$. That is, the vector $\mathbf{l}$ has to be perpendicular to both $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$, and the cross product between $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ provides such a vector.
concepts.motivation_md: Determining the unique line connecting two points is a fundamental task in geometry; homogeneous coordinates reduce this problem to a simple cross-product operation.
concepts.recap_md: - The line $\boldsymbol{l}$ connecting points $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ is given by $\boldsymbol{l} = \mathbf{p}_1 \times \mathbf{p}_2$.

concepts.title: Intersection of Two Lines

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: The intersection point of two lines in homogeneous coordinates is found by taking the cross product of the vectors representing the lines.
concepts.content: Given two lines $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_2$, the intersection point between them is the cross product: $$\mathbf{p} = \boldsymbol{l}_1 \times \boldsymbol{l}_2$$ (see figure: Using homogeneous coordinates to get the line that passes by two points, and to obtain the intersection of two lines. Both operations are analogous.) The coordinates of $\mathbf{p}$ computed this way will be in homogeneous coordinates. To get the actual point coordinates in heterogeneous (Cartesian) coordinates, you must divide by the third component.
concepts.motivation_md: Finding where two lines meet is a common problem in computer vision and graphics. Homogeneous coordinates allow this to be solved using the same cross-product logic used to find lines from points.
concepts.recap_md: - The intersection point $\mathbf{p}$ of lines $\boldsymbol{l}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{l}_2$ is $\mathbf{p} = \boldsymbol{l}_1 \times \boldsymbol{l}_2$.

concepts.title: Colinearity Condition

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: Three points are colinear if the determinant of the matrix formed by their homogeneous coordinate vectors is zero.
concepts.content: If three 2D points are colinear, then the determinant of the matrix formed by concatenating the three vectors, in homogeneous coordinates, as columns is equal to zero: $\det( [\mathbf{p}_1~\mathbf{p}_2~\mathbf{p}_3 ])=0$. Similarly, if three lines intersect in the same point, we have a similar relationship: $\det( [\boldsymbol{l}_1~\boldsymbol{l}_2~\boldsymbol{l}_3 ])=0$.
concepts.motivation_md: This condition provides a simple algebraic test to verify if points lie on a single line or if multiple lines are concurrent at a single point.
concepts.recap_md: - Points are colinear if the determinant of their concatenated homogeneous vectors is zero.

slots.motivation: This condition provides a simple algebraic test to verify if points lie on a single line or if multiple lines are concurrent at a single point.
slots.key_passage: - Points are colinear if the determinant of their concatenated homogeneous vectors is zero.

concepts.title: Plane Equation in Homogeneous Coordinates

position.section_title: Lines and Planes in Homogeneous Coordinates

concepts.one_liner: A 3D plane is represented in homogeneous coordinates by a vector such that its dot product with any point on the plane is zero.
concepts.content: We can represent planes in 3D using a method analogous to 2D lines. The equation of a 3D plane is $aX+bY+cZ+d=0$, which can be written in homogeneous coordinates as: $$\mathbf{\pi}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{P} = 0$$ where $\mathbf{\pi} = [a,b,c,d]^\mathsf{T}$ are the plane parameters and $\mathbf{P}=[X,Y,Z,1]^\mathsf{T}$ are the 3D point homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.motivation_md: Extending homogeneous coordinates to 3D allows for a consistent algebraic framework to handle points and planes, mirroring the simplicity of 2D point-line operations.
concepts.recap_md: - A 3D plane is defined by the vector $\mathbf{\pi} = [a,b,c,d]^\mathsf{T}$.

slots.motivation: Extending homogeneous coordinates to 3D allows for a consistent algebraic framework to handle points and planes, mirroring the simplicity of 2D point-line operations.
slots.key_passage: - A 3D plane is defined by the vector $\mathbf{\pi} = [a,b,c,d]^\mathsf{T}$.
slots.example: We can represent planes in 3D using a method analogous to 2D lines. The equation of a 3D plane is $aX+bY+cZ+d=0$, which can be written in homogeneous coordinates as: $$\mathbf{\pi}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{P} = 0$$ where $\mathbf{\pi} = [a,b,c,d]^\mathsf{T}$ are the plane parameters and $\mathbf{P}=[X,Y,Z,1]^\mathsf{T}$ are the 3D point homogeneous coordinates.

concepts.title: Forward Mapping
concepts.one_liner: Forward mapping transforms an image by applying a transformation to each source pixel and recording its color at the resulting destination coordinates.
concepts.content: Forward mapping is an algorithm for transforming an image where every pixel in the original image, represented as $[\ell_i,x_i,y_i]$, has a transformation $\mathbf{M}$ applied to its coordinates. The pixel color is then recorded into the resulting coordinates in the target image. (see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping using nearest neighbor interpolation. Forward mapping will produce missing values.) As coordinates might result in non-integer values, the result can be rounded to the closest pixel coordinate using nearest neighbor interpolation. While intuitive, forward mapping is generally not a good idea because it produces artifacts such as missing values and aliasing. (see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping. Forward mapping produces many artifacts. In both cases we use nearest neighbor interpolation.)
concepts.motivation_md: Forward mapping is the most intuitive approach to image warping, but it is rarely used because it often leaves 'holes' in the destination image when source pixels do not map to every target pixel.
concepts.recap_md: - Forward mapping iterates through source pixels and maps them to the destination.

concepts.title: Backward Mapping
concepts.one_liner: Backward mapping iterates over target image pixels and uses the inverse transformation to sample color values from the source image.
concepts.content: (see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping using nearest neighbor interpolation. Forward mapping will produce missing values.) The best approach for image warping is backward mapping, which consists of looping over all the pixels of the target image and applying the inverse geometric transform, $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$. Interpolation is then used to get the correct color value from the source image. This process guarantees that there will be no missing values, provided the coordinates stay within the input image frame. To avoid aliasing, blurring the input image might be necessary if the target image has a lower pixel density than the input. (see figure: Comparison between forward and backward mapping. Forward mapping produces many artifacts. In both cases we use nearest neighbor interpolation.)
concepts.motivation_md: Backward mapping solves the 'missing value' problem of forward mapping by ensuring that every pixel in the destination image is assigned a color sampled from the source.
concepts.recap_md: - Backward mapping iterates through destination pixels and uses the inverse transform $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ to find source colors.

slots.motivation: Backward mapping solves the 'missing value' problem of forward mapping by ensuring that every pixel in the destination image is assigned a color sampled from the source.
slots.key_passage: - Backward mapping iterates through destination pixels and uses the inverse transform $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ to find source colors.

concepts.title: MIP-mapping
concepts.one_liner: MIP-mapping uses a multiscale image pyramid to efficiently determine the best neighborhood for high-quality interpolation during image warping.
concepts.content: MIP-mapping is a technique for high quality and efficient interpolation. It relies on a multiscale image pyramid to efficiently compute the best neighborhood structure needed to perform the interpolation at each location. This technique is particularly useful when warping an image onto a curved surface.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard interpolation can be slow or cause aliasing when scaling images; MIP-mapping uses pre-calculated image scales to make the process both faster and visually smoother.
concepts.recap_md: - MIP-mapping utilizes a multiscale image pyramid for efficient interpolation.

prereq.rationale: The homogeneous representation of a line as a vector depends on the definition of points in homogeneous coordinates.

The intersection technique treats lines as vectors, which is established in the homogeneous line equation definition.
The resulting intersection point is in homogeneous coordinates and must be converted back to Cartesian coordinates for standard use.
The condition for colinearity is based on points sharing the same homogeneous line vector.
Representing a 3D plane in this form requires the use of 4-element homogeneous coordinate vectors for 3D points.
Translation in homogeneous coordinates is represented as a matrix-vector product, which requires the definition of the homogeneous coordinate system.
The shearing transformation is defined using a 3x3 matrix acting on homogeneous coordinates.
Chaining transformations involves multiplying the matrices of individual operations, including the translation matrix in homogeneous form.
Chaining transformations includes the shear matrix as one of the fundamental components that can be combined.
A Euclidean transformation is defined as the result of chaining specific types of transformations (rotations and translations).
Implementing transformations as convolutions requires representing the image as a set of pixels with explicit geometry.
Scaling invariance is a defining property of how homogeneous coordinate vectors represent points in space.
The conversion technique operates on homogeneous vectors to extract their standard coordinate values.
The goal of this technique is to recover the standard Cartesian (heterogeneous) representation of a point.
The conversion process (dividing by the last dimension) is justified by the scale invariance of the projective representation.
STNs rely on parametric image transformations, such as affine transformations, to manipulate the input data spatially.
To maintain differentiability for backpropagation, STNs typically implement their spatial warping using backward mapping and interpolation.
Warping in this context is performed by evaluating the learned implicit functional representation of the image at specific coordinates.
Warping with implicit representations uses the inverse geometric transformation to sample from the continuous function, which is a form of backward mapping.
The mathematical formulation for warping with implicit representations utilizes homogeneous coordinates to apply the inverse transformation matrix.

Projective transformations are a more general set of mappings than affine transformations, utilizing all 8 degrees of freedom in a 3x3 matrix.
Elations are a specific subset of transformations described by the full 3x3 projective matrix.
Heterogeneous coordinates are conventional Cartesian descriptions contrasted with the augmented homogeneous representation.
The STN provides a learned, end-to-end method for performing image alignment within a deep learning pipeline.
Implicit image representations are a specific implementation of the continuous function view of images, where the function is typically learned from data.

Image alignment is defined as the reverse problem of image warping: identifying the transformation rather than applying it.
